MI-2025-HB4011.s: The bill would let the state’s budget department transfer or sell certain state-owned land in Arenac County, including land now under the corrections department. It sets rules for how the land could be sold or moved, gives local governments a chance to buy it, and requires some uses to stay public if sold below market value. Money from a sale would go to the state treasury and then to the general fund.

MI-2025-HB4135.s: The law lets the state sell or give Jackson County up to about 81 acres of former landfill land that is under the Department of Corrections. Jackson County gets first chance to buy it for $1 for two years after the law takes effect, and any sale to a local government must be for public use, meaning use by the public or by local government for things like parks, schools, or law enforcement. If the land is sold, the money left after sale costs goes to the state general fund.

MI-2025-HB4301.s: Michigan has enacted a law that expands the definition of an authorized emergency vehicle. It adds certain vehicles used by the Michigan Mutual Aid Box Alarm System and, in some emergencies, vehicles from a federally recognized nonprofit charity. The law also changes which vehicles may use certain emergency lights, affecting fire, police, ambulance, and some rescue and aid vehicles.

MI-2025-HB4302.s: The law creates an exception to commercial driver license rules for authorized emergency vehicles used by the Michigan Mutual Aid Box Alarm System. It affects people who operate those emergency vehicles. It took effect on October 5, 2026.

MI-2025-HB4598.s: The law adds gift card fraud to Michigan’s organized retail crime rules. It makes it a crime to get, alter, tamper with, or use a gift card or gift card redemption info with intent to defraud and to get money, goods, or services from it. The law keeps organized retail crime a felony with up to 5 years in prison, a $5,000 fine, or both, and it takes effect January 3, 2027.

MI-2025-HB4599.s: Michigan law now adds definitions tied to gift card fraud in the state’s organized crime law. It defines terms such as gift card, gift card redemption information, issuer, and seller for use in that law. The change affects people and businesses involved with gift cards and organized retail crime cases. The act takes effect January 3, 2027.

MI-2025-HB4678.s: The bill would set rules for selling motor fuel to people who rent certain fuel-powered equipment, like generators, lifts, and similar mobile equipment. It would let the rental business charge a flat fee or a per-gallon fee written in the rental contract, and it would require the fuel to meet federal air rules and the fuel meter to be checked at least every 3 years. The renter could not be forced to buy fuel from the rental business, and the act would take effect only if House Bill 4679 also becomes law.

MI-2025-HB4679.s: This bill would change parts of Michigan’s weights and measures law. It would set inspection and testing rules for weights and measures used in selling goods and services, including sample testing for some devices and a special rule for qualified dispensers. It would also update sale, packaging, labeling, and device standards for commodities, and it would keep some cottage food labels from needing the operation’s address if certain conditions are met. It says motor vehicle repair facilities would stay under secretary of state oversight for certain oil-related issues unless the matter is referred to the department.

MI-2025-HB4793.s: The bill would remove the rule that school board members must file an acceptance of office after they are elected or appointed. It would affect people elected or appointed to school boards in Michigan. The bill also says it would take effect only if two related bills are also enacted into law.

MI-2025-HB4794.s: The bill would remove the rule that community college board of trustees members must file an acceptance of office. It would also remove failure to file that acceptance as a reason a trustee’s seat becomes vacant. The change would affect people elected or appointed to community college boards in Michigan.

MI-2025-HB4795.s: The bill would remove the rule that appointed intermediate school board members must file a written acceptance of office and proof that they are eligible within 7 days after appointment. It would affect school board members appointed to help run a consolidated school district, and it would only take effect if House Bill 4793 also becomes law.

MI-2025-HB5121.s: The bill would remove the cost for serving papers for personal protection orders. It would affect people who ask for or are served with these orders, and the court and law enforcement agencies that handle service. The bill also adds new sections to state law on this process.

MI-2025-HB5356.s: Passed bill would change Michigan vehicle title rules for dealers and related vehicle businesses. It would add a rule for a "courtesy transportation vehicle" and update several dealer record and business location requirements. It would also change what information is needed when a vehicle title is transferred or issued.

MI-2025-HB5514.s: Michigan now bars youth transport companies from using blindfolds, hoods, handcuffs, chains, and other restraints on young people being taken to certain youth residential treatment programs, with a narrow exception for serious, immediate danger. The law also limits pickups for this kind of transport to between 6 a.m. and 9 p.m. A person who breaks the law can be fined up to $1,000.

MI-2025-HB6007.s: The bill would change Michigan food law on who handles food service inspections and licensing. It would shift some duties to local health departments, keep some powers with the state for certain food processing, and limit local rules in some cases. It would also add and update several license exemptions for certain small, temporary, and low-risk food businesses, including some sales by minors and some prepackaged food sellers.

MI-2025-HB6033.s: The bill would raise many fees that process servers can charge for serving court papers, including summonses, subpoenas, eviction papers, and seizure orders. It would also raise some related costs, like mileage-linked fees, photo checks, mail service, and extra charges for wrong addresses or electronic filing. It would bar fees for serving papers in extreme risk protection order cases, and it would keep some personal protection order service costs paid from a state fund instead of by the person asking for service.

MI-2025-HB6080.s: The bill would change rules for teacher hiring and staffing decisions in Michigan public schools. It would require school boards to use clear procedures and use job performance as a factor, and it would not let length of service be the only factor in those decisions. It would also set rules for what school courses can count toward pay or salary advances, using only certain accredited college credit with letter grades.

MI-2025-HB6243.s: The bill would change Michigan rules that bar large investment firms from buying single-family homes. It adds more types of allowed sales, including some rent-to-own, rehab-to-rent, and homeownership programs, and some sales tied to foreclosures, housing plans, or older holdings. It would still limit large investors from buying single-family homes in the state unless a listed exception applies.

MI-2025-HB6259.s: The bill would change Michigan’s sentencing rules for criminal sexual conduct offenses. It affects people convicted of those crimes, along with related assault and robbery offenses listed in the sentencing chart. The change would take effect 90 days after it becomes law, if the linked bills also become law.

MI-2025-HB6260.s: The bill would change the penalties for first-degree criminal sexual conduct, which is a serious sex crime, under Michigan law. It would affect people convicted of this offense, including cases involving young victims, force, weapons, injury, or abuse of authority. If enacted, it would take effect 90 days after it becomes law.

MI-2025-HB6262.s: The bill would change the penalty for criminal sexual conduct in the third degree in Michigan. It would lower the minimum prison term from 15 years to 5 years, while keeping a possible maximum of life in prison.

MI-2025-HB6263.s: The bill would change the rules for fourth-degree criminal sexual conduct in Michigan by restating when sexual contact counts as that crime, including cases involving age gaps, force or threats, mental incapacity, family ties, school staff, special education students, and certain child care or foster care settings. It would also set the penalty for that offense as a felony punishable by up to 2 years in prison, a fine of up to $500, or both. If enacted, the change would take effect 90 days later.

MI-2025-HB6282.s: The bill would bar former Michigan legislators from taking jobs with an entity that gets a grant from the utility consumer participation board for at least 2 years after leaving office. It would also make a violation a misdemeanor, with up to 90 days in jail, a fine of up to $1,000, or both. The House passed the bill with immediate effect.

MI-2025-HB6302.s: The bill would require each public school building to have a United States flag, a flag staff, and the needed equipment to display it. It would also require the flag to be displayed at the school during school hours, except during inclement weather. In classrooms or other instructional sites where pupils recite the pledge of allegiance, it would require a smaller United States flag to be displayed in a prominent location.

MI-2025-HB6309.s: This bill would name a portion of M-86 in Branch County the "Casey Rice Memorial Highway." The named stretch runs from the intersection of M-86 and US-12 west to the intersection of M-86 and Arbogast Road.

MI-2025-HB6425.s: The bill would let petition circulators use a village name or a postal city on the circulator certificate instead of a city, village, or township name in some cases. It would affect people who gather signatures for nominating petitions in Michigan.

MI-2025-HB6426.s: The bill would set new rules for local review of large-scale data centers, which are big facilities used for servers and data storage. It would require developers to give local governments detailed project information, post most of it for public review, and let local governments ask for more details and recover their review costs. It would also limit when people can challenge local decisions in court and allow fines for material misstatements. The act would take effect 90 days after it becomes law, but only if House Bill 6427 also becomes law.

MI-2025-HB6427.s: The bill would make parts of Michigan’s zoning law subject to the data center local decision protection act. It would also tie zoning board of appeals review to that act when someone appeals a zoning decision in circuit court. The bill would not take effect unless House Bill 6426 becomes law.

MI-2025-HB6428.s: The bill would change Michigan rules on vehicle size, weight, and load limits. It would update axle weight limits and seasonal road weight limits, and it includes rules for farm haulers and public utility vehicles on certain roads. It also keeps the state and local road agencies involved in setting and approving permits and exemptions for some heavier loads.

MI-2025-HB6429.s: The bill would change Michigan’s solid waste law to add a definition for coal combustion residuals, which are left over from burning coal, and set rules for how those materials can be used or handled. It also would update many related terms in the state’s environmental protection law, including several kinds of beneficial use, or allowed reuse, of ash and other waste materials.

MI-2025-HB6430.s: The bill would change the rules for getting or renewing many Michigan occupational licenses and registrations. It would set a 90-day deadline for the department to issue an initial or renewal license after a complete application is filed, with shorter 30-day timing for real estate brokers and associate brokers, and it would require refunds or a 15% fee cut if the deadline is missed. It would also spell out late renewal, reinstatement, and military-duty exemption rules for licensed workers and registrants, and it would affect many occupations listed in the bill.

MI-2025-HB6431.s: The bill would create a state grant program to help local governments, tribes, and some nonprofits study flood risks and plan flood-resilience projects before disasters happen. It would fund things like flood studies, wetland and floodplain restoration, culvert inventories, and related work, with grants covering up to 75% of costs and set dollar caps. The department would set rules, review applications, post project reports online, and send yearly reports to lawmakers and the governor.

MI-2025-HB6432.s: The bill would require state House and Senate members to follow the reporting rules for people in the Healthy Michigan Plan, and to do any required community engagement work by January 1, 2027. If a lawmaker does not comply, a public employer could not pay for that member’s medical benefit plan until they do. It would affect state legislators and the public employers that help pay for their health coverage.

MI-2025-HB6433.s: The bill would create a fast court process for a property owner to challenge a recorded document that the owner believes fraudulently claims title to real estate. It would let the owner file an affidavit with the county register of deeds, mail notice to the other parties, and then ask the circuit court to review the claim if no counter affidavit is filed within 35 days. It also sets out what a court petition must include and says the state court office would make forms for the process.

MI-2025-HB6434.s: Would give property owners protection from having their property tax value reset higher while they are trying to fix a title problem. It would apply to Michigan property tax assessments and change state tax law rules for those cases.

MI-2025-HB6435.s: The bill would let a person who was a victim of deed theft sue in circuit court over real property taken without their approval or through fraud. If they win, they could recover $5,000, three times their actual losses, and reasonable lawyer fees. It would affect owners of residential or commercial property, and it would take effect 90 days after becoming law.

MI-2025-HB6436.s: The bill would change Michigan's time limit for filing libel or slander claims and would add a new rule for slander of title cases. A slander of title case would have to be filed within 3 years after the latest of when the false property claim is found, when a law enforcement investigation ends, or when any related criminal case is finished. It would affect people bringing these kinds of court cases in Michigan.

MI-2025-HB6437.s: The bill would create a state tax credit program for sales or rentals of farm assets to new farmers. It would let the agriculture department certify beginning farmers and approve credits for owners who sell or rent land, livestock, buildings, or machinery to them. The credits would be capped at $32,000 for a sale, up to $7,000 a year for a cash rent deal, and up to $10,000 a year for a share-rent deal, with a $5 million yearly cap for the program. It would also require an annual report on the program starting June 1, 2028.

MI-2025-HB6438.s: The bill would create a state income tax credit for owners of farm assets who sell or rent those assets to a beginning farmer. It would apply to tax years starting on or after January 1, 2027, and the credit would be limited to the amount on a state tax credit certificate. People claiming it would need to attach the certificate and, for rental deals, proof that the agreement was active.

MI-2025-HB6439.s: Michigan’s campaign finance law would be changed to add transparency rules for paid political ads. It would affect people and groups that pay for those ads.

MI-2025-HB6440.s: The bill would pause the extra tax on wholesale marihuana for one year after the law takes effect. It would affect marihuana businesses such as growers, retail licensees, and provisioning centers that sell or transfer marihuana. After that year, the tax would apply again at the rates already set in state law.

MI-2025-HB6441.s: The bill would bar pawnbrokers from taking a firearm as pawn. It would also bar second-hand dealers and junk dealers from offering or displaying a firearm for sale if they accept one. A person who breaks this rule would commit a misdemeanor.

MI-2025-HB6442.s: The bill would require the state labor director to set workplace safety rules for workers exposed to heat or hot work areas. The rules would cover employer heat plans, indoor and outdoor heat checks, water and rest breaks at set temperature levels, worker training, reporting heat illnesses and deaths, and protection from retaliation for reporting heat hazards. It would also allow some employers to be exempt and require the director to publish the reported data.

MI-2025-HB6443.s: The bill would require hospitals to give an emergency medical screening and stabilizing treatment to people who ask for it or who appear to need urgent care. It would also require hospitals to keep a log of these cases, not ask about ability to pay before giving emergency care, and follow set rules before moving or discharging a patient who is not stable. The bill also sets duties for on-call physicians and bars them from making false statements about a patient’s condition or the transfer rules.

MI-2025-HB6444.s: This bill would change who serves on the Michigan sentencing commission and how members are appointed. It keeps members from the legislature, the attorney general's office, judges, law enforcement, prosecutors, defense attorneys, victims' services, mental or behavioral health, and the department of corrections. It also changes the rules for the member who was previously incarcerated to a member who was convicted of a felony in this state and served at least 5 years in a department of corrections facility, and it sets appointment and vacancy rules for commission seats.

MI-2025-HB6445.s: This bill would let the board accept a physician’s national certification as meeting continuing education requirements for license renewal. It applies to both physicians and osteopathic physicians. The bill also keeps the requirement for a certain number of hours or courses in pain and symptom management.

MI-2025-HB6446.s: This bill would require landlords to complete and send a rental property database form to the Michigan State Housing Development Authority for each rental property they own. The form would ask for property location, the number of rental units, landlord contact information, beneficial owners, and certain compliance statements, and landlords would have to update it after a change of ownership. Landlords would also have to give the form to tenants, post the latest copy in a common area, and attach it to renewal leases. A landlord who violates the section could face a civil fine of up to $50 per day, and the measure would not take effect unless two other bills are enacted into law.

MI-2025-HB6447.s:
This bill would require the state housing authority, with help from the department of technology, management, and budget, to create and maintain a rental property database. The database would be free and publicly available on the authority’s website.

Landlords who own and operate rental property in Michigan would have to submit a form with information for the database. The bill applies to landlords before and after the effective date of the act.

MI-2025-HB6448.s: This bill would require a landlord who owns and operates a residential rental property in Michigan but does not live in Michigan to name an in-state agent. The agent would be allowed to conduct business with the tenants on the landlord’s behalf. A landlord who breaks this rule could be fined up to $1,000, and the county prosecutor or attorney general could seek the fine.

MI-2025-HB6449.s: The bill would provide $5 million from the state general fund for a rental property database. It directs the Michigan State Housing Development Authority to create and maintain the database and a form for landlords to submit information about rental property in Michigan. The database must be publicly accessible and free to use, and the money cannot be spent unless two other bills are enacted into law.

MI-2025-HCR10.s: This resolution sets the legislative schedule for the House and Senate. It says both chambers would adjourn on Thursday, November 12, 2026, and return on Tuesday, December 1, 2026, at the times listed in the resolution.

MI-2025-SB102.s: The bill changes the rules for county treasurers when people ask for transcripts, abstracts, copies, or statements from records on file. It sets fees for paper records and creates a separate rule for requests for electronic copies of records. For electronic records, the bill sets a maximum charge and says the records must be sent in an electronic format with defined fields, and copies may not be resold for a commercial purpose.

MI-2025-SB1026.s: The bill would change the rules for Michigan domestic credit unions that use an assumed name, or a name other than their legal one. It would require notice to the state before using a new assumed name and let the state block or stop a name that is confusing or misleading. Credit unions using an assumed name would also have to show both names clearly in signs, ads, mailings, and key account papers.

MI-2025-SB1027.s: The bill would change the rules for how members of a domestic credit union can amend its bylaws or charter, which is the basic set of rules for the credit union. It would let members approve those changes, give or take back power from the credit union board to make them, and require notice of any such proposal before the meeting. Changes would still need review and approval by the director, except for bylaw changes that are only logistical.

MI-2025-SB1029.s: The bill would change notice rules for some credit union closures. It covers when a credit union closes its main office or branches because of an emergency, and it says the credit union must notify the state director and any other government office required by law.

MI-2025-SB1030.s: The bill would change the notice rules for credit union members when a merger is put to a vote at a special meeting. It affects domestic credit unions and their members, and the notice would need to be given in the time set by the revised law. The bill also keeps the state director involved in approving merger plans.

MI-2025-SB1113.s: This bill would revise the rules for getting and renewing a certified public accountant certificate in Michigan. It changes the education, experience, and exam requirements for applicants, and it also updates the rules for out-of-state CPAs who want practice privileges in this state. The bill would require continuing education for license renewal and peer review for firms and sole practitioners that provide audits, reviews, or certain compilations.

MI-2025-SB1132.s: The bill would create a Camp Grayling improvement fund in the state treasury to receive Camp Grayling revenue, gifts, grants, and investment earnings. The Department of Military and Veterans Affairs could use the money, if approved, for repairs, upgrades, environmental cleanup, lodging, roads, utilities, training support, and related planning, and it could also collect fees and enter leases and contracts for Camp Grayling. It would require yearly reports on the fund and projects, and it would take effect 90 days after it becomes law.

MI-2025-SB1134.s: The bill would let certain state workers choose to leave the Tier 2 retirement plan and join the Michigan state police retirement system. It applies to some eligible civil service workers, conservation officers, and certain state police officers, and it sets a window in 2027 for making that choice. It also lets some of those workers move part or all of their retirement contributions to buy service credit in the state police system.

MI-2025-SB1192.s: The bill would set new rules for prison hearings and for when the corrections department can place some prisoners in solitary confinement. It would create a hearings division, give prisoners notice and a chance to present evidence, and require help for prisoners with disabilities or limited English. It would also limit solitary confinement for certain prisoners, set time limits, and require medical and mental health reviews in some cases.

MI-2025-SB1194.s: This bill would repeal section 682b of the Michigan vehicle code. That section is about passengers riding in the open bed or cargo area of a pickup truck. It would affect rules for people riding in pickup trucks.

MI-2025-SB1196.s: The bill would change how some vacant county offices are filled in Michigan. In counties with an elected county executive, that executive would join the county clerk and prosecutor in naming a replacement for most empty county offices, instead of the probate judge. A county clerk or prosecutor vacancy would still be filled by the circuit court judges. The change would take effect only if SB 1195 also becomes law.

MI-2025-SB1197.s: This bill would bar certain military and federal officers and personnel from bringing or keeping armed individuals at places where an election is being held, unless force is needed to repel armed enemies of the United States. It would also bar them from setting voter qualifications, stopping qualified voters from voting, ordering election officials to accept illegal votes, changing election rules, or interfering with election officials. Violations could lead to criminal penalties, and a person harmed by a violation could bring a civil lawsuit.

MI-2025-SB1198.s: The bill would add sentencing guidelines for certain Michigan election crimes, including unauthorized presence or conduct by military or some federal officers at or during an election. It would affect how judges sentence people convicted of those offenses. The change would take effect only if Senate Bill 1197 also becomes law.

MI-2025-SB1199.s: The bill would require paid social media posts about candidates or ballot questions to show who paid for them, with the committee, agent, or contractor’s name and address. It would also require a committee to report the name and street address of anyone paid to help support or oppose a candidate or ballot question on social media. The rules would apply to people, committees, and other entities that create or first publish these posts, and they include civil fines for violations.

MI-2025-SB1201.s: The bill would create a Michigan animal agriculture alliance to set up and run a grant program for animal research, working with the state agriculture department, Michigan State University, and industry representatives. It would also create a new animal research fund in the state treasury to hold and pay out grant money. The legislature would have to put at least $3 million into the fund each year, and any money left in the fund at the end of the year would stay there.

MI-2025-SB1202.s: The bill would change state spending for fiscal year 2026-27 and give $2.5 million to the Michigan animal agriculture alliance through the agriculture department. It also cuts $1.5 million from the labor and economic opportunity department and $1 million from the natural resources department. The text says the new spending rules would apply to these appropriations and that some prior spending authority would end.

MI-2025-SB1203.s: The bill would change the rules for graduated driver licenses for people 17 years old or younger. It would allow a person who is at least 15 years and 9 months old to get a level 1 graduated licensing status if they meet the listed school, vision, health, driving time, and parent approval requirements. It would also set the requirements for level 2 and level 3 status, including driver education, driving experience, and restrictions on when and with whom a person may drive.

MI-2025-SB1204.s: The bill would change Michigan’s driver training law and add a new section with more rules. It would update the legal definitions for driver training, instructors, and related terms, and it would set or change what a driver training provider must submit to get certified. The changes would affect driver education providers, instructors, and people taking teen, adult, or commercial driver training.

MI-2025-SB1205.s: This bill would set aside $1,000,000 from the state general fund for the Department of State Police. The money would be awarded to Michigan Mutual Aid Box Alarm System to support Michigan Task Force 1 in urban search and rescue efforts. It also says the funds must be spent in line with federal rules and regulations.

MI-2025-SB1206.s: This bill would repeal Michigan’s Local Government Labor Regulatory Limitation Act, also known as 2015 PA 105. It would remove that law from the state code.

MI-2025-SB1207.s: This bill would repeal the Fair and Open Competition in Governmental Construction Act, also known as 2011 PA 98. It would affect the law governing governmental construction in Michigan.

MI-2025-SB1208.s: The bill would change how long a driver can keep an election to opt out of no-fault personal injury protection coverage. The election would stay in place while the person keeps insurance with the same insurer or an affiliate, unless the person revokes it in writing. If the person loses the required health coverage, they would have 30 days to get new coverage that includes that protection.

MI-2025-SB1209.s: The bill would bar the Michigan National Guard from being sent into active duty combat unless Congress has declared war or taken another official action to call up the state militia. It would apply only if 25 or more states pass a similar law. The governor would have to take the steps needed to follow this rule.

MI-2025-SB1210.s: The bill would change rules for money collected under agricultural marketing programs. It would require any money from those assessments to be refunded to the people who paid it if it is still held more than 10 years after it was received. Programs already breaking this rule on the bill's effective date would have 2 years to return the money.

MI-2025-SB1211.s: The bill would require public water suppliers to notify the state and the public when their water does not meet drinking water standards. It would also require a public advisory within 3 business days after a lead action level exceedance is found, and the state would have to post a searchable public database with violation and test results by January 1, 2028. The bill would also require a public hearing within 30 days after a significant deficiency notice, followed by a public notice and at least a 30-day comment period.

MI-2025-SB1212.s: The bill would let the state sell or transfer a 2.13-acre state-owned parcel in Detroit, in Wayne County, known as part of the former Michigan State Fairgrounds. It sets rules for how the property could be sold, including bidding, auction, sale to a local government, or transfer to the state land bank authority, and it requires any sale proceeds, after certain costs, to go to the state’s general fund. If the land is sold with limits for public use or with mineral rights conditions, those rules would stay with the property.

MI-2025-SB1213.s: The bill would create a new state program that gives family leave and family and medical leave insurance benefits to certain workers in Michigan. It would set the reasons leave could be used, require employer and employee contributions, and require employers to help with claims and other duties. It would also bar discrimination and retaliation tied to using these rights and set up a state fund and claims process.

MI-2025-SB1216.s: This bill would change the time limit for filing a libel or slander lawsuit. It would also add a new rule for slander of title claims, requiring them to be filed within 3 years of the latest of three listed dates. These changes would affect people bringing those kinds of court actions.

MI-2025-SB1217.s: This bill would create a court process for a real property owner to challenge a recorded document that the owner says fraudulently claims to transfer title or an interest in the property. The owner would file an affidavit and send notice to the grantor and grantee, and the grantor or grantee would have a chance to file a controverting affidavit. If no timely controverting affidavit is filed, or if the court finds the document did not convey title or an interest, the circuit court can make findings and enter an order. The bill also sets out what must be included in the filings and what documents must be attached to the petition.

MI-2025-SB1218.s: This bill would let a victim of deed theft sue a deed thief in circuit court over real property. A victim could recover five thousand dollars, three times the actual damages, and reasonable attorney fees. The bill defines deed theft as taking, transferring, or encumbering title to residential or commercial real property without the owner's approval or knowledge, or through fraudulent or deceitful means.

MI-2025-SB1221.s: This bill would give county prosecutors the first chance to act as co-counsel in certain child protection cases that involve the prosecution of an individual for a crime listed under the Child Protection Law. If the prosecutor refuses, the Department could hire outside counsel to serve as co-counsel. The measure affects child protective services cases that need judicial proceedings and cases with a child suspected of abuse or neglect.

MI-2025-SB1223.s: This bill would change Michigan school policy on seclusion and restraint in public schools. It would prohibit solitary seclusion and bar several forms of restraint and other practices, while allowing emergency seclusion or physical restraint only as a last resort to prevent serious harm. It would also require school districts to follow state policy, document each use, report it to parents or legal guardians, and develop plans for pupils who show a repeated pattern of behavior.

MI-2025-SB17.s: This bill would designate the new moon day on the eighth lunar month as a holiday in Michigan. It would be known as “Diwali,” “Deepavali,” or the “Festival of Lights.” The holiday is described as one celebrated by Hindus, Jains, and Sikhs.

MI-2025-SB198.s: This act regulates how motor vehicle dealers, manufacturers, and third parties collect, share, use, and store protected dealer data. It limits when manufacturers and third parties can access dealer data systems, and it requires prior express written consent for many uses of protected dealer data. The act also sets rules for dealer data vendors and authorized integrators, including open access methods, termination, data transfer, and dealer audit rights.

MI-2025-SB265.s: The bill would require at least 1% of certain Michigan transportation funds to be spent on nonmotorized transportation, like bike and walking paths, and it would let that money be used for building, improving, maintaining, or repairing those facilities. It would also set rules for when these features must be added during road projects and for 5-year plans by the state, counties, cities, and villages that get this funding. Snow removal would not count as maintenance under this bill.

MI-2025-SB413.s: The bill would change the Michigan board of psychology from 9 voting members to 11 voting members. It would reduce the number of public members and add 2 psychologists with limited licenses to the board. The bill would also change the rules for limited licenses for psychologists with a master's degree, including supervised experience requirements and when they may practice without supervision.

MI-2025-SB433.s: The law requires the state health department to create and update a notice about the risks of tobacco, vaping, nicotine products, THC cannabis products, and synthetic intoxicating hemp. It must include prevention and treatment help, plus signs of THC poisoning and what to do if someone shows those signs. Schools must give the notice to parents or guardians and post a link to it on their website, and the notices may be sent by email or mail. The law took effect on October 5, 2026.

MI-2025-SB478.s: This law authorizes the state administrative board to transfer a state-owned parcel of land in Livingston County from the department of corrections to the department of military and veterans affairs. The transfer is permanent once approved and once written notice is given to both departments. The department of military and veterans affairs must reimburse survey costs and other closing costs tied to the transfer.

MI-2025-SB712.s: The bill would change who can be appointed as a district court magistrate in Michigan. It would require a magistrate to live in, or be employed by, the county where they are appointed, with some rules also applying in adjoining districts. The bill also keeps current rules about how magistrates are appointed and how they may serve in other counties or districts.

MI-2025-SB791.s: This bill would name a portion of I-475 in Genesee County the "St. John Street Community Memorial Highway." It applies to the stretch of highway starting at Hamilton Avenue and continuing north to one-quarter mile north of Stewart Avenue.

MI-2025-SB947.s: The bill would update Michigan dam safety rules for inland lakes and other dams. It would require dam owners to register their dams in stages over five rounds, starting 6 months after the act takes effect, and to submit plans, inspections, and other safety documents. It would also tighten who can prepare dam plans and set new rules for reviews, renewals, and department approval of registrations.

MI-2025-SB979.s: The bill would require retirement system trustees, called investment fiduciaries, to follow written ethics and training rules. Those rules would include at least 8 hours of professional training and education every 2 years for each trustee. It would apply to the trustees who manage public employee retirement system investments.

MI-2025-SB980.s: The bill would ban people from installing or running cryptocurrency kiosks, which are machines that let people buy, sell, or swap crypto for regular money. It would also bar owners, renters, and others who control a place from letting one operate there. A first violation could bring a civil fine of $2,000 to $5,000, and later violations could bring $5,000 to $10,000.

MI-2025-SCR16.s: The resolution honors John Pappageorge, a former member of the Michigan House and Senate, and offers condolences to his family. It recalls his military service and his work in state and local government. The Senate adopted it on 2026-10-14, and copies would be sent to his family.

MI-2025-SR141.s: Adopted by the Michigan Senate, this resolution asks the U.S. State Department to report on the abduction and military-style training of Ukrainian children by Russia. It also asks Congress to set aside money to help return the children to Ukraine. The resolution asks the U.S. government to make their return a priority in talks.

MI-2025-SR142.s: This resolution recognizes October 13, 2026, as Homeschool Day in Michigan. It says parents and legal guardians have the right to choose homeschooling as a legitimate educational alternative for their children. It also recognizes homeschooling families and says homeschooling is an important part of the state’s educational landscape.

MI-2025-SR143.s: This resolution commemorates October 4-10, 2026, as Fire Prevention Week in Michigan. It says home fires, working smoke alarms, and fire safety are serious concerns, and it points to the risks from lithium-ion batteries in everyday devices. It also notes that first responders work to reduce home fires and injuries through prevention, protection, and education.

MI-2025-SR144.s: The Michigan Senate adopted a resolution to designate September 15 through October 15, 2026, as Hispanic Heritage Month. It is a formal statement honoring the histories, cultures, and contributions of Hispanic and Latino Americans. The date applies to Michigan and the month-long observance in 2026.

MI-2025-SR145.s: The Senate adopted a resolution recognizing October 1, 2026, as Auto Heritage Day. It honors Michigan’s auto history and the people, companies, inventors, and workers who helped shape the industry. The resolution also notes the role of the MotorCities National Heritage Area and its work to preserve and promote that history.

MI-2025-SR147.s: The Michigan Senate adopted this resolution to designate November 2026 as Military Family Appreciation Month. It expresses support and gratitude to servicemen and women, their families, and veterans, and sends a copy to the Michigan Department of Military and Veterans Affairs.
